Chapter 2: The Struggle to Survive and the Cost of Small Choices
Imagine waking up every single day to a world where survival is never guaranteed. Life in Auschwitz was exactly that—a constant fight against hunger, exhaustion, and a kind of despair that seeped into your bones. Each morning started with the piercing sound of whistles, and the frantic rush to line up for roll call, no matter if the wind was biting or rain was pouring down. The cold felt endless, especially when all you had was a thin uniform that barely kept you warm.
Food? It was almost nonexistent—a watery soup, maybe a hard crust of bread, and sometimes, not even that. Bodies grew weaker with each passing day, but what was truly remarkable was how the will to survive kept people moving forward.
In this world, even the smallest decisions could change everything. Picture this: someone offers you a slightly bigger piece of bread if you do them a favor, or maybe a spot closer to the warmth of the stove if you promise to keep quiet about something you saw. On the surface, these seem like little things. But in Auschwitz, they could mean the difference between life and death.
The problem was, every privilege came at a price. If you took that extra bread, someone else would go without. If you traded for a warmer place to sleep, you might be turning your back on someone who needed it just as much. Every day, people had to weigh their own survival against the needs of others, and there were no easy answers.
There’s one story that sticks out—a woman put in charge of handing out bread in her barrack. She knew she could give a little more to her best friend, but doing so meant shortchanging someone else. The guilt was constant, but so was the fear of losing the only person she could trust. Then there was the offer of a job in the camp’s administration—a role with better food and lighter duties. But the catch? You’d have to work alongside the guards, sometimes even helping to enforce the rules. Suddenly, the line between victim and collaborator started to blur, and the shame of those choices lingered long after.
Still, there were people who tried to hold onto their sense of right and wrong. Maybe a group of friends would promise to share everything equally, no matter the temptation. But hunger and fear have a way of eroding even the strongest bonds. Arguments broke out over scraps of food, and sometimes, friendships that had lasted for years just ended in silence. Trust was everything—and yet, it was so fragile.
But even in the middle of all this suffering, there were moments of compassion. Someone might come across an extra potato and quietly pass it to a sick friend, knowing it could save a life. A handful of women took turns caring for a child whose mother had disappeared, pooling together what little they had to keep her alive. These acts of solidarity, even if brief, gave people a break from the daily struggle and a glimpse of hope.
The camp had a way of revealing who people really were. Some, when given a bit of power, used it to protect and help others. Maybe a barrack leader would look the other way if someone broke a rule to help a friend get food. Others, worn down by fear and hunger, became harsh and unkind. The system was designed to turn people against each other—and it often did. But just as often, it showed that even in the worst conditions, people could still choose kindness.
Over time, surviving became almost routine. People learned to read the guards’ moods, to hide their own weakness, to tuck away a little bread for later. The camp taught its own hard lessons—about resilience, about what it costs to compromise, and about how people adapt to things they once thought unimaginable.
The choices people made in Auschwitz were never simple, and the memory of those decisions stayed with them long after liberation.
